scenarios.name: Before any hand starts, nobody holds cards and hand_number is 0
Hand 1 deal empties the 24-card deck and each player holds 6 (chance-independent)
Hand 1 passing: every seat chooses two cards and still holds 6 afterwards
Hand 1 pass to the left keeps every hand at 6 cards
Hand 2 pass to the right keeps every hand at 6 cards
Hand 3 pass across keeps every hand at 6 cards
After passing, every hand still holds 6 cards and the deck is empty
Hand 4 has no pass and every hand holds 6 cards
Passing completes and play continues with full hands
First trick of hand 1: each seat plays one card, leaving 5 each
Later tricks are led and played: after 3 tricks each seat holds 3 cards
In a trick every player plays exactly one card face up
Leader may play any card: the trick completes with 5 cards left each
Following suit when able: all 6 tricks are played out legally
A void player may play any card: the hand plays out to empty hands
Each trick is decided and a full hand of 6 tricks is played
Trick points and counts are reset to 0 after the hand is scored
Normal scoring: the hand is scored and its counters reset (chance decides the scores)
Reversis scoring: the hand is scored and its counters reset (chance decides whether a reversis happens)
End of hand resets hand points and trick counts to 0
Game ends after hand 4 is scored; seat 1, far ahead, wins whatever the deal
Lowest total wins: seat 3 at 0 against 100s cannot be caught in the last hand

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 4 seats. The deck of 24 cards deals exactly 6 to each of 4 players, the left/right/across passing needs exactly 4 seats, and the 15-point reversis payment is set for 3 opponents.
The source has no table talk. Adding it would add a mechanic, and in a trick game it would leak hidden hands.

spec_choices.what: One script round equals one hand (deal, pass, then 6 tricks run by a repeat)
spec_choices.why: The source's 7 rounds per hand (1 pass + 6 tricks) map onto one script round, and the game ends after 4 such rounds, giving 28 source rounds in all.

spec_choices.what: Cards coded as rank+suit text (e.g. 'JH'), with rank values A=6, K=5, Q=4, J=3, 9=2, 8=1 for comparing
spec_choices.why: Finding the trick winner needs a number to compare; these values keep the source order A > K > Q > J > 9 > 8.

Players pass away dangerous high cards and the Quinola, then duck under the led card and discard point cards when void. A player with a very strong hand may instead aim to win all 6 tricks for a reversis, so opponents must watch for it and take one trick to stop it.

simplifications.what: Passing 2 cards is two simultaneous polls of one card each
simplifications.why: A question takes a single choice from a list. The second poll excludes the first card, and no card moves until both polls are done, so passing stays simultaneous and secret.

simplifications.what: The winner is computed as the highest of 0 - total, and a tie at the lowest total is a shared result
simplifications.why: The engine ranks by highest value and shares ties at the top. This matches 'lowest total wins, a tie for lowest is a draw'.

variation.original_summary: Reversis is a four-player trick-taking game with no trumps in which players try to avoid winning tricks that contain counting cards (A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1), and the Jack of Hearts (Quinola) is especially dangerous. The player with the fewest points wins, unless someone takes every trick (the reversis), which reverses the aim and wins outright.

review.evidence: Always playing the lowest legal card loses to a player who dumps high counters when void of the led suit. Always playing high takes most of the points. The reversis threat stops 'just dodge everything' from being safe, because if all three others duck, one strong hand can sweep. The anticlockwise lead gives no lasting edge over a full deal. A single deal can favour whoever holds low cards.

Card counting, reading voids and timing discards are real skills. But one deal of 13 cards is heavily luck-driven: a hand full of high cards in long suits can hardly avoid points. The original gives no mechanism, such as passing or several hands, to average this out.

Weak players still score, since points are spread around. Strong players improve through inference about voids, by holding back or forcing out the Quinola, and by spotting or blocking a reversis attempt. It is not solved.
Hands are hidden. Players must infer holdings from what others follow and discard, keep track of which counters are out, and plan several tricks ahead, both for safe exits and for or against a slam.
Trick winners follow from suit and rank. Points are card sums. Lowest total wins. Pools, side payments and the various Quinola bonus variants are messy, but they are still arithmetic.

The game is turn-based, text-only and has hidden hands, which all fit. However, 13 tricks with 52 cards, stakes, pools and several regional variants are too long and loosely specified. A deck that small per round and fixed rules are needed to stay within the step and round limits.

problems: A single long deal makes the result depend heavily on the cards dealt (luck swamps skill).
52 cards and 13 tricks per deal is too long for the round limit once several deals are played to reduce luck.
Pools, talon payments, side payments and the variant Quinola bonuses are underspecified and not a winner rule the engine can use.
There is no decision before play that lets a player fix a bad deal, so the deal often decides the game before any reasoning happens.
The reversis reward ('wins outright, sweeps pools') is not stated as numbers, so its risk and reward cannot be weighed.

changes.what: Use a 24-card deck (A K Q J 9 8 in four suits) and deal 6 cards each, so a hand is 6 tricks.
changes.why: This keeps the full rank and counting structure, including the Quinola, while making a hand short enough to play several.
changes.fixes: 52 cards and 13 tricks per deal is too long for the round limit once several deals are played to reduce luck.

changes.what: Play 4 hands. The first lead rotates so that each seat leads first exactly once. Penalty points carry over between hands.
changes.why: Averaging over 4 deals and equal lead order reduces deal luck and seat advantage. It also creates multi-hand planning, such as pushing points onto the current leader.
changes.fixes: A single long deal makes the result depend heavily on the cards dealt (luck swamps skill).

changes.what: Before each hand except the 4th, every player at the same moment secretly passes 2 cards: to the left in hand 1, to the right in hand 2, across in hand 3, and no pass in hand 4.
changes.why: Passing lets good players repair a bad deal. It also creates hidden knowledge to exploit, since you know two cards an opponent holds and they know two of yours, and it opens the option to build toward a reversis.
changes.fixes: There is no decision before play that lets a player fix a bad deal, so the deal often decides the game before any reasoning happens.

changes.what: Fix the scoring: A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1 per card taken, with the Quinola (J of hearts) worth 5 instead of 1. The total is 44 per hand. The winner is the player with the lowest total after 4 hands.
changes.why: This gives one exact, arithmetic objective with no pools or payments.
changes.fixes: Pools, talon payments, side payments and the variant Quinola bonuses are underspecified and not a winner rule the engine can use.

changes.what: Reversis: a player who takes all 6 tricks of a hand scores 0 for that hand, and each other player scores 15 instead of their card points.
changes.why: This keeps the reversal with a stated payoff that is large but not game-ending. The three others must sometimes take a counter on purpose to break a sweep, which creates conflict among them.
changes.fixes: The reversis reward ('wins outright, sweeps pools') is not stated as numbers, so its risk and reward cannot be weighed.

keeps: Trick-avoidance with no trumps and strict follow-suit.
The counting cards A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1, with the lowest score winning.
The Quinola (Jack of Hearts) as the special dangerous card.
The reversis: taking every trick reverses the aim and punishes everyone else.

recommendation.reason: The core trick-avoidance game rewards inference and planning. It only needs a smaller deck, several hands, passing and fixed scoring to fit and to reduce luck.

variation.name: Short Reversis
variation.summary: A four-player no-trump trick-avoidance game over 4 hands of 6 tricks each, with secret card passing, a Quinola worth 5, and a reversis (taking all 6 tricks) that hands 15 points to each opponent. The lowest total wins.
variation.rules:
DECK: 24 cards, A K Q J 9 8 in each of the four suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs). Rank within a suit, high to low: A, K, Q, J, 9, 8. There are no trumps.

SEATS: Players 1 to 4 sit in a circle. Play goes from player 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 and back to 1. 'Left' means the next player in that order, 'right' the previous, and 'across' the player two seats away.

GAME STRUCTURE: The game is 4 hands. Each hand is 7 rounds: one passing round followed by 6 trick rounds. That makes 28 rounds in total.

PASSING ROUND (first round of each hand):
(1) The deck is shuffled and each player is dealt 6 cards, seen only by that player.
(2) In hands 1, 2 and 3, all players at the same moment each secretly choose 2 cards from their hand to pass. The passes go left in hand 1, right in hand 2 and across in hand 3. Passed cards are added to the receiver's hand after everyone has chosen, and only the passer and receiver know which cards moved. In hand 4 there is no pass.
(3) The game announces that passing is complete.

TRICK ROUNDS (6 per hand):
- Lead: In the first trick of hand h, player h leads (player 1 in hand 1, player 2 in hand 2, and so on). In every later trick, the winner of the previous trick leads.
- Playing: Starting with the leader and going around in seat order, each of the 4 players plays one card face up. The leader may play any card. Each other player must play a card of the led suit if they hold one. If they hold none, they may play any card.
- Winning: The highest card of the led suit wins the trick. Cards of other suits never win.
- Recording: The trick winner adds the trick's points to their score for this hand. Points per card: A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1, with the Jack of Hearts (Quinola) worth 5. Nines and Eights are worth 0. The winner's trick count for the hand goes up by 1. All played cards are public.

END OF HAND (after the 6th trick):
- If one player won all 6 tricks (a reversis), that player scores 0 for the hand and each other player scores 15 for the hand.
- Otherwise each player scores the points they took. These always total 44 across the four players.
- Hand scores are added to running totals, which are public. Hand scores and trick counts reset to 0.

END OF GAME: After the 4th hand, the game ends.
variation.objective: After 4 hands, the player with the lowest running total wins. If two or more players tie for the lowest total, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Averaging over four hands, equal first leads and passing to repair bad deals should make card reading and planning matter more than the deal. Passing creates targeted inference: you know two of a neighbour's cards, can pass a dangerous Quinola or Ace into a likely void, or can keep strength to try a reversis. The reversis threat stops pure ducking: when one player is sweeping, someone among the other three must take a counting trick to stop it, and each would prefer that someone else pays. This is a real conflict among the opponents. Across hands, players should steer points toward whoever leads the running totals. Simple policies lose: always playing the lowest legal card lets voids be exploited and lets a sweeper go unchecked, always playing the highest card collects most of the 44 points, and random play is beaten by any counting player. Talk is left out. Its main use would be loose ganging-up deals among three players, which the engine cannot enforce. Play order, the card passes and the cards played already carry the signals that are worth reasoning about, and talk would add steps without adding a decision.

balanced.evidence:
ARITHMETIC: Each suit holds A4+K3+Q2+J1 = 10, so four suits make 40. The Jack of Hearts is worth 5 instead of 1, adding 4, for 44. The stated total of 44 is correct. A reversis scores 0 for the shooter and 3x15 = 45 for the others. With an ordinary hand averaging 11 per player, a reversis is a swing of about +15 relative to each opponent. That is large but rare.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule (lowest total wins, a tie for lowest is a draw):
(a) 'Always play the highest legal card' wins most tricks it contests, eats about 20+ of the 44 points per hand, and loses almost every game.
(b) 'Always play the lowest legal card; when void, discard the highest-value card' is the obvious heuristic, not a dominant strategy. It still loses when dealt many high cards with no low guards, because after the pass you must follow suit. It cannot see when to duck versus win a cheap trick to take the lead. Sensible players beat it by voiding a suit through passing and dumping the Quinola and Aces onto it. It does not avoid loss against every opponent action.
(c) 'Always lead or play the first listed option' depends on option order and amounts to random play. It loses to card counters.
(d) 'Always attempt a reversis' fails whenever any opponent holds one card higher in a led suit. It then usually leaves the player holding many point cards, which is heavily punished.
No option is strictly better whatever opponents do. Following suit is forced, and whether ducking is right depends on the other cards held.

SEAT AND ORDER: The first lead rotates (player h leads hand h), so each seat leads one hand. Passes go left, right, across, then none, which is symmetric over 4 hands. Later leads are earned by winning tricks. No seat has a structural edge, and all four players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS: The deck, ranks, follow-suit rule, trick winner (highest card of the led suit, no trumps), lead rules, pass timing and direction, pass visibility, scoring, the reversis condition, end of game and tie handling are all specified. Passes are chosen simultaneously, so a player cannot pass a card just received. Hands stay at 6 cards. All 24 cards are dealt, so there is no unseen talon.

FINITE AND ARITHMETIC: The game has exactly 28 rounds. Scores are sums of card values the game records, and the winner is the minimum total, which needs calc but nothing more.

LIMITS:
- Steps: 13 of 20.
- Choice steps: 4 of 4. A trick round has 4 sequential card plays. The passing round has 1 simultaneous poll, gated by a 'when' condition on the round index, which is allowed.
- Attributes: 12 of 20.
- Hidden elements: 1 of 3 (the hands).
- Random draws: 1 per round (the deal, only in the passing round).
- Rounds: 28 of 40.
The follow-suit legality check is a complex rule check that a referee model can rule on. Trick winner and points are calculable. There is no board, clock, trading or binding agreement.

TALK: None, which is sensible. Trick play itself is the information channel (cards played reveal voids and holdings). Talk would be either cheap and unenforceable collusion against the leader or mere words. Players can reason from public played cards and known passes rather than guess blindly.

The game is not a repeated cooperation dilemma, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
INFERENCE AVAILABLE: All 24 cards are in play, and each player knows 6 cards plus the 2 they passed. Counting the played cards narrows the remaining holdings each trick, and voids are revealed when a player fails to follow. By trick 4 or 5 the remaining distribution is largely deducible.

PLANNING: The pass lets a player void a suit or shed Aces and the Quinola, but sending dangerous cards to a specific neighbour has consequences. During play a player must decide when to duck, when to take a cheap trick to seize the lead, when to dump the Quinola (5 points) on an opponent's trick, and whether to block a reversis attempt at low cost.

CHANCE ESTIMATE: The deal decides perhaps 35–45% of the outcome over 4 hands. A hand full of Aces and Kings with no low cards is costly. Passing 2 of 6 cards and the choice of discards give good players real control.

EQUAL GOOD PLAY: When all four play well, the deal decides more of the result, as in any trick-taking game. But a bad deal can be mitigated by passing and voiding, so the deal is not the sole determinant.

SKILL GAP: A counting player who plans voids should clearly beat the 'lowest card' heuristic and random play over 24 tricks.

design_flags_left: the built game has 6 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4

triage.reason: The rules make the first round of each hand the passing round, with the 6 trick rounds coming after it. After `rounds: 1` each player should therefore still hold 6 cards (dealt, then 2 passed and 2 received), which is exactly what the game showed: deck empty, every hand 6 cards, trick_number 0. The tests wrongly expect every hand to be empty after only one round.
triage.guidance:
Keep to the round structure: round 1 of a hand is deal plus pass, and rounds 2 to 7 are the 6 tricks.
- After 1 round, expect the deck lens at 0 and each player's hand lens at 6. That is chance-independent, because passing 2 and receiving 2 keeps 6.
- To check that all cards are played out, run 7 rounds (a full hand). Then expect every hand lens at 0 and hand_number 1. Also expect the trick results to fit the scoring: the sum of hand scores added to totals is 44, or it is the reversis pattern 0/15/15/15.
- Do not assert on internal bookkeeping such as stage, pick, offer or trick_number.
- Do not predict which cards are dealt or passed, since chance decides them.

triage.reason: The game was built correctly, but the design needs 6 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4. The extra steps come from the passing choice plus four trick plays in seat order starting from a leader who changes. Against random seats the results are also lopsided, with seat 4 winning 21 games and seat 2 only 10.
triage.guidance:
Cut the choice steps per round to 4 or fewer.

1. Drop the passing round entirely. Each hand becomes 6 trick rounds, so 24 rounds in total. Remove pass_count and last_passing_hand, and set rounds_per_hand = 6 and total_rounds = 24.

2. Restructure each trick as two choice steps instead of four turns that rotate with the leader:
   - First, the leader plays one card face up. This is a single sequential choice by the current leader.
   - Then the other three players choose their cards at the same moment, as a simultaneous poll. They must follow the led suit if able, otherwise they may play any card.
   - The highest card of the led suit wins and takes the points, as now.

3. Keep the leader rotation: player h leads the first trick of hand h, and the trick winner leads after that. Keep the reversis rule (0 for the taker, 15 to each other player) and lowest-total-wins.

Because nobody gains an advantage from playing late, the simultaneous follow should also reduce the seat-order bias that favoured seat 4. Re-check balance against random seats after the change.
